# ADR-002: Use PostgreSQL for Production Database

| Date | Status | Deciders | Related | Confidence |
|------|--------|----------|---------|------------|
| 2026-09-11 | Proposed | Product, Engineering | FEAT-recipe-share | High |

## Context

| Aspect | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| Problem | Production must serve concurrent writes from many users (recipe posts, ratings, comments, saves). SQLite serializes all writes behind one file lock, so concurrent publishers queue and time out. |
| Current State | ADR-001 selected SQLite for MVP with a planned post-launch move to PostgreSQL. ADR-001 was still Proposed; TD-recipe-store is still draft; no production SQLite data exists (assumption, see Risks). |
| Requirements | PRD §Constraints: concurrent multi-user writes without a global lock. FEAT-recipe-share NFR: 100 concurrent publishers without 400+ errors. TD-recipe-store: ≤ 20 submissions/min, ≤ 1000 concurrent reads, POST p99 ≤ 500ms. PRD: ship in 6 months, infrastructure under $5k. |
| Decision Drivers | Operator statement (2026-09-11): "move from SQLite to Postgres for production multi-user concurrency". Avoid a post-launch data migration under load. Keep ops overhead low by using a managed service. |

## Decision

We will use PostgreSQL (version 16 or later) on a managed service as the single relational database for all environments, starting before launch, and drop the SQLite path entirely.

**Key Points**: MVCC gives concurrent readers and writers without a global lock | One dialect across dev, staging, prod (the TD schema already uses `UUID`, `gen_random_uuid()`, `VARCHAR`) | Managed service supplies backups, TLS, and failover | Application connects through a bounded connection pool

## Alternatives

| Option | Pros | Cons | Evaluation |
|--------|------|------|------------|
| Keep SQLite, add app-side write queue | Zero ops; no cost; already decided in ADR-001 | Still one writer; queue adds latency under burst; per-server file blocks horizontal scaling; post-launch migration under live load | Rejected: does not meet the concurrent-write constraint; defers the same migration to a riskier moment |
| SQLite in WAL mode with `busy_timeout` | Readers no longer block on writers; small change | Writes still serialize; ~10-20 writes/sec ceiling from ADR-001 stays; single-host only | Rejected: improves reads, not the multi-writer problem |
| MySQL / MariaDB (managed) | Multi-writer; widely hosted; comparable cost | Team familiarity lower; weaker JSON and UUID ergonomics; TD schema written in PostgreSQL dialect | Rejected: no advantage over PostgreSQL for this workload; would force schema rework |
| Firebase / Firestore | Serverless; auto-scales | Vendor lock-in; limited relational queries (joins for ratings, comments, saves); export friction | Rejected: same reasons as ADR-001 |
| **PostgreSQL (managed)** | MVCC concurrency; mature tooling; TD schema already PostgreSQL dialect; managed backups and TLS; $10-50/mo (ADR-001 estimate) | Managed service cost; connection limits require pooling; local dev needs a running PostgreSQL (Docker) | **Selected: meets the concurrency constraint at a cost inside the PRD budget with the least schema and tooling change** |

## Consequences

| Type | Impact |
|------|--------|
| Positive | Concurrent writes from many users without lock queuing; no post-launch database migration; one SQL dialect everywhere; point-in-time recovery and automated backups from the provider |
| Negative | Recurring managed-service cost; connection-pool sizing becomes an operational concern; local development and CI need a PostgreSQL instance instead of a file; migrations run against a network database |
| Neutral | Single primary per environment (dev, staging, prod), matching the PRD "no read replicas" constraint; backup story moves from file copy to provider snapshots |

## Risks

| Risk | Prob | Impact | Mitigation |
|------|------|--------|------------|
| Production SQLite data already exists and needs migrating (assumption: none exists, based on ADR-001 Proposed and TD draft status) | Low | Medium | Before cutover, confirm with Engineering; if data exists, write an export/import runbook as follow-on work before this ADR moves to Accepted |
| Connection pool exhaustion under burst | Medium | Medium | Bounded pool per API instance; `statement_timeout`; expose pool wait metrics; add PgBouncer if instance count grows |
| Managed provider not yet chosen (PRD lists AWS, Vercel, or equivalent) | Medium | Low | Provisional: any provider offering PostgreSQL 16, automated backups, and TLS satisfies this ADR; provider choice is guidance-needed from infra and does not change the decision |
| Cost overrun beyond ADR-001's $10-50/mo estimate | Low | Low | Start on the smallest production tier; review monthly spend against the $5k PRD budget |
| Provider outage or primary failure | Low | High | Automated daily snapshots with RTO ≤ 1 hour (carried from ADR-001); enable provider multi-AZ when budget allows |

## Validation

| Success Metric | Review Trigger |
|----------------|----------------|
| 100 concurrent publishers complete POST /recipes with zero 5xx or lock/timeout errors (FEAT-recipe-share NFR) | Reconsider pooling or tier if any lock or timeout errors appear in staging load test |
| POST /recipes p99 ≤ 500ms, GET /recipes p99 ≤ 100ms (TD-recipe-store) | Reconsider tier or indexing when p99 exceeds target for 7 consecutive days |
| Pool wait time p99 < 50ms | Add PgBouncer or raise pool size when exceeded |
| Monthly database spend ≤ $50 | Review tier when exceeded |

## Supersession

- **Supersedes**: ADR-001 (Use SQLite for Initial Database)
- **Superseded by**: None

## Concern Impact
